newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - BAA profits from passenger growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - BAA profits from passenger growth.

text.p: British airports operator BAA Plc announced a 10.2 percent rise in underlying profits on Monday and said strong passenger growth was continuing, with traffic expected to be up by over five percent in the current year.

The company also said it would go on spending 450 million pounds to 500 million pounds ($700-800 million) a year on facilities, despite delays in starting the 1.5 billion pound project to build a fifth terminal at London Heathrow.

Profits before exceptionals rose to 444 million pounds ($724.7 million) for the year to March 31, up 41 million pounds on a year ago. The final dividend was increased 10.9 percent to 7.9 pence to give a total payout of 12.4p for the year.

However, earnings fell 6.6 percent to 28.4 pence a share due to a write-off of some preliminary costs for the Terminal Five (T5) project, which pushed down pre-tax profits to 407 million pounds, from 418 million pounds last time.

BAA announced in April that delays in the protracted public planning inquiry for Terminal Five had forced it to stop capitalising interest on preparatory expenditure, but it said it would continue to capitalise actual costs.
As a result it booked a 40 million pound exceptional charge to write off the accumulated interest previously capitalised and pay an additional 13 million pounds of interest charges.

The company said it would continue to invest strongly in new capital projects, spending 496 million pounds last year, and planning to go on spending 450-500 million pounds every year for the next 10 years.

Finance director Russell Walls said the T5 delays would not cut spending because it would reschedule other work, particularly at its two other London airports, Gatwick and Stansted, where traffic was set to grow at a faster rate because of constraints at Heathrow.
The share price rose 1 1/2 pence to 539 in early afternoon trading after the results, which were generally in line with analysts' predictions.
"The actual numbers were broadly in line with thinking," said Selwyn Jones, London-based transport analyst at Credit Lyonnais.

The company said 98 million passengers passed through its seven British airports last year, up 4.6 percent on a year ago, which fuelled a 9.6 percent increase in turnover to 1.373 billion pounds from retailing, airport charges and property rentals.
"Passenger growth was good at 4.6 percent and we believe that the current year will see growth of over five percent," chief executive Sir John Egan said.

"At our airports costs remained firmly under control with efficiency improvements in both operating and construction costs continuing," Egan said. "The base for building shareholder value is a solid one."
Retail revenue was up nine percent at 606 million pounds as BAA managed to persuade passengers to spend more waiting for their flights in its airport shopping arcades.
Average retail income per passenger grew six percent to 4.36 pounds per passenger although BAA warned that the strength of sterling had slowed growth in the second half of the year.

BAA's revenue from airline user charges which are regulated by the Civil Aviation Authority rose 7.6 percent to 467 million pounds, while its property interests generated another 252 million pounds of revenue.
However, the company declined to comment on the prospects of it being made liable to the new Labour government's proposed windfall tax on excess profits made by former state-owned utilities.
Labour has declined to say precisely which companies will be hit ahead of Chancellor Gordon Brown's budget on July 2, an uncertainty which has overshadowed BAA's share price in recent months.

"That has certainly been depressing it slightly," said analyst Kevin Fogarty at Daiwa Europe. "It is rather uncertain as to whether it (BAA) will be a victim. It looks likely but the actual extent of it is not certain."
Previously BAA has said it did not think it should be liable, denying that it has made any excess profits since being privatised 10 years ago.

"We have said everything we want to say about the windfall tax," finance director Russell Walls told Reuters. "We don't think we should be liable and we want to leave it (comment) at that for today." ($ = 0.612 British Pounds)
